pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: The business is adequate to strong because margins are high and the base is spread over eleven markets, but nearly all recent growth was bought. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 45.9% for nine months 2026, down from 47.3%, and postpaid customers were 30.79% of mobile customers against 21.10% a year earlier, which makes revenue more recurring. Reported revenue rose 55.2% while organic growth was 4.4%, so the larger scale mostly reflects Coltel, Ecuador and Uruguay and favourable currency moves rather than a stronger market position. The consequence for creditors is that earnings quality has to be judged on the organic rate and on how much of the acquired EBITDA turns into cash. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 28; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 33; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation C01; calculation C02

Leverage is moderate on the statements but has risen faster than the headline suggests. Net debt before derivatives was USD 7,800 million, or 2.05x last-twelve-month reported EBITDA, at 30 September 2026, against 1.83x at the end of 2025. Pro forma net debt would be USD 8,379 million, or 2.20x, once the dividend payable of USD 579 million is settled in cash from the October 2026 instalment onwards, and the 15 October 2026 Coltel loan swap leaves it at USD 7,800 million, or 2.05x; pro forma cash after the dividend settlement is not established. The issuer's own net leverage, which adds derivatives and vendor financing, deducts lease costs and is pro forma for acquisitions, was 2.53x against 2.17x at the end of 2025. A lease liability of USD 3,190 million and capital expenditure payables of USD 2,101 million sit outside debt, so creditors face more fixed claims than the ratio shows. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C06; calculation C07; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 32

Cash generation is solid but largely distributed, so deleveraging depends on the dividend as much as on operations. Equity free cash flow was USD 867 million, up 36.0% from USD 638 million, yet it equals only 29.31% of Adjusted EBITDA against 32.48% a year earlier, mainly because lease payments of USD 483 million and finance charges of USD 432 million together took 30.93% of Adjusted EBITDA against 28.26%. Declared dividends of USD 755 million were 0.87x equity free cash flow and left only USD 112 million, so cash cannot reduce debt materially while the payout continues. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 31; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 5; calculation C03; calculation C04

Liquidity is the weakest dimension. Cash of USD 848 million was 0.97x the USD 872 million of debt due within one year, against 4.72x at the end of 2025, with USD 986 million due in the following year, and the USD 600 million revolving facility matures in October 2027 with its availability after 2025 not established. Funding access is nonetheless real: during 2026 the group raised development-bank and bond funding, reopened its 2032 senior notes and added bank loans in several countries, and the annual report records a Moody's rating of Ba2 with a stable outlook and a Fitch rating of BB+ at year-end 2025. The consequence is that refinancing depends on market and bank access staying open for about USD 1,858 million over two years, with no committed cushion shown for the period after 2025. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 25; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 24; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 255; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 273; calculation C08

Earnings are concentrated, and currency moves flatter reported growth. Guatemala and Colombia together supplied 58.69% of segment revenue and 56.01% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, and the annual report states that group cash flow is highly dependent on Guatemala. The Colombian peso, Paraguayan guarani and Bolivian boliviano rose 25.4%, 22.7% and 17.1% against the US dollar over the year, which lifted reported results, while costs, capital expenditure and 38.99% of debt are in US dollars. A reversal would cut earnings in dollars, partly offset by a smaller dollar value of local-currency debt, but would leave dollar debt and dollar costs unchanged. Basis: 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 62; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 44; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 17; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 33; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 32; calculation C09; calculation C10; Business & governance (CP-1A)

Financial policy is the main judgemental drag, consistent with a Medium sponsor and governance risk. One family group holds 42.2% of the voting shares and four of eight directors are affiliated with it, shareholders approved dividends of USD 3.00 per share payable to April 2027 and the board added an interim USD 1.50 per share, and the senior management plan communicated in October 2026 rewards equity free cash flow of USD 2 billion with no leverage condition stated. Policy therefore leaves the outcome for creditors to the board's discretion rather than to a documented restriction. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 20; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 28

Colombia is the swing factor for the next two years. It is now the largest segment at 38.37% of segment revenue but earned a nine-month Adjusted EBITDA margin of 38.65% against 56.09% in Guatemala, after one-off costs of USD 116 million in nine months, and it faces competitors with substantially greater resources, including América Móvil, and a regulator that may impose asymmetric rules on a larger market share. If integration savings arrive the margin gap narrows and cash conversion improves; if competition forces price cuts the gap persists on the largest revenue base. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 17; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 41; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 37; calculation C06; calculation C10

runs.text: The first strength is margin. Adjusted EBITDA margin of 45.9% for nine months 2026 means each dollar of revenue leaves a large cushion for lease, interest and tax charges, which is why interest cover stays at 4.58x despite higher debt; the margin is down from 47.3% a year earlier on acquisitions, so the cushion is thinner than before. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 41; calculation C01; Financial foundation (CP-1)

The second strength is a more recurring revenue base. Postpaid customers rose to 30.79% of mobile customers, and prepaid customers, who buy short packages and sign no contract, are being migrated, which supports revenue visibility and lowers churn exposure in Guatemala, Panama and Paraguay. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 33; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 35; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 79; calculation C02

The third strength is funding access matched to local revenue. 61.01% of gross debt is in local currencies, and 2026 saw a development-bank bond, a reopening of the 2032 senior notes and local bank loans, so the group can raise money across currencies, which reduces the risk that one market closes refinancing. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, pages 24–25; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 32; calculation C09

The fourth strength is rising cash generation. Equity free cash flow rose 36.0% to USD 867 million, guidance for 2026 was raised to around USD 1.1 billion, and issuer net leverage fell from 2.73x to 2.53x in the third quarter, which shows that operations can reduce leverage when dividends are covered. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 31; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 29; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 32

The first weakness is concentration. Guatemala and Colombia supply 56.01% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, so a shock in either market reaches the cash that services debt and funds dividends. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 17; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 62; calculation C10

The second weakness is liquidity against maturities. Cash of USD 848 million is 0.97x the debt due in a year, so the group relies on refinancing and on a revolving facility whose availability is not established. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 25; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation C08

The third weakness is distributions: declared dividends were 0.87x equity free cash flow, which slows deleveraging and lets a controlling shareholder's priorities shape credit outcomes. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 20; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 31; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C03

The fourth weakness is fixed claims outside debt. Lease liabilities of USD 3,190 million and capital expenditure payables of USD 2,101 million raise charges that do not flex, and lease payments plus finance charges took 30.93% of Adjusted EBITDA against 28.26%. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 3; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 31; calculation C04; Financial foundation (CP-1)

The fifth weakness is the quality of growth. Reported revenue rose 55.2% against 4.4% organically, integration cost USD 149 million of one-off items in nine months and acquired businesses have provisional accounting, so a faster slowdown than organic trends would be a surprise only to those reading reported growth. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 28; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 41; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 10

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: Between October 2025 and April 2026 the group completed six acquisitions or buy-outs that together changed its scale, and it sold most of its tower portfolio. Uruguay (enterprise value USD 440 million, closed 7 October 2025) and Ecuador (enterprise value USD 380 million, closed 30 October 2025) added mobile operators and their debt and leases. In Colombia the group bought out its partner's UNE shares for about USD 571 million on 29 January 2026, acquired Telefonica's 67.5% of Coltel for about USD 214.4 million on 6 February 2026, of which USD 169 million had been paid at that date, and bought the remaining Coltel shares on 27 April 2026. Coltel brought USD 1,424 million of other debt and financing and USD 515 million of lease liabilities. Basis: 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 212–213; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, pages 8–10; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 5

The Chile entry in February 2026 was a joint acquisition with NJJ Cactus, a partner the filings do not describe as related: the vehicle paid USD 50 million at closing, carries contingent earn-outs without recourse to Millicom that the annual report caps at USD 150 million and the nine-month report at USD 490 million, and has an outstanding earn-out liability of USD 110 million funded by the vehicle's own debt. On the disposal side, the Lati tower sale to SBA and Atis Group brought total consideration of about USD 975 million and a gain of USD 741 million but created about USD 680 million of new lease assets and liabilities, and the sale of the Paraguay mobile finance business was agreed in January 2026 for a base price of USD 10 million. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 11; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 297; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 214; 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, page 12

New debt in 2026 included a COP 370,000 million eight-year private bond subscribed by the Inter-American Development Bank and Proparco on 27 March, an USD 87.5 million reopening of the 2032 senior notes on 14 April, and a series of variable-rate loans at Coltel and Tigo Colombia, while Tigo Paraguay redeemed its 2027 senior unsecured notes for about USD 139.7 million on 29 April. The debt effects are measured by Financial foundation; the governance point here is that most new borrowing sits at operating companies in local currency and some carries parent guarantees. Basis: 6-K_2026-11-05_dp256407_6k.htm.jsonl, pages 23–25; 20-F_2025-12-31_tigo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 124

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Control rests with one family group, and creditors should read every capital decision with that in mind. Atlas Investissement, ultimately owned by the Niel family, held 42.2% of the voting shares excluding treasury shares at 31 December 2025, and the Niel family group reported 44.1% including shares it expected to buy by 30 June 2026. Four of eight directors are affiliated with it, the company is not a controlled company under Nasdaq rules because the holding is below 50%, and the annual report itself says the holder can influence director elections and corporate actions. The consequence for creditors is that dividend, acquisition and related-party decisions can reflect the shareholder's priorities, while the board's audit committee, which is wholly independent, is the main check.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Shareholder distributions are large against current earnings and absorb most free cash flow. Declared dividends were USD 1,048 million in 2025, against net profit attributable to owners of USD 1,316 million, and USD 755 million in nine months 2026, against net profit attributable to owners of USD 316 million and equity free cash flow of USD 867 million, so declared dividends were 0.87x equity free cash flow. A dividend payable of USD 579 million sat on the balance sheet at 30 September 2026 and the board states a policy of sustaining or growing dividends while maintaining a prudent capital structure. The mechanism is that payouts competing with acquisition funding and debt repayment for the same cash leave little retained cash to reduce leverage, and dividends are limited to distributable reserves, with USD 757 million of retained profits at 30 September 2026 not distributable.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Acquisitions have changed the perimeter faster than the disclosure can follow. The group bought Uruguay and Ecuador in October 2025 for enterprise values of USD 440 million and USD 380 million, completed the buy-out of its Colombian partner for about USD 571 million on 29 January 2026, closed the purchase of Coltel on 6 February 2026 for about USD 214.4 million, and bought the remaining Coltel shares on 27 April 2026. Reported nine-month revenue rose 55.2% while organic growth was 4.4%, Coltel's and Ecuador's purchase accounting is provisional, and management excluded Uruguay and Ecuador from its 2025 internal control assessment. The consequence is integration and restructuring cost, with Colombia carrying USD 116 million of one-off costs in nine months, and growth figures that cannot be read like for like.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Earnings are concentrated in two countries. Guatemala supplied 20.32% of consolidated segment revenue and 24.34% of consolidated segment Adjusted EBITDA in nine months 2026, and Colombia, now two segments, supplied 38.37% and 31.67%, so the two together are 58.69% of revenue and 56.01% of Adjusted EBITDA. The annual report states that the group's cash flow is highly dependent on Guatemala. The consequence is that a regulatory, currency or competitive shock in either country would reach the cash that services debt and funds dividends.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Related-party exposure to the controlling shareholder's group is small in flows but has two features worth monitoring. The balance sheet showed USD 195 million payable to the Iliad Holding group at 31 December 2025 against USD 2 million a year earlier, and the filings do not state what it is. Separately, the Chile acquisition in February 2026 was made through a vehicle owned 49% by Millicom and 51% by NJJ Cactus, which the filings do not describe as a related party although its name matches the NJJ Holding that the related-party note says Xavier Niel owns, with a Millicom call option in the fifth and sixth years and a later option for the partner to buy Millicom's interest. The consequence is that any later funding of those options or of the vehicle's losses, which already exceed Millicom's recognised interest by USD 41 million, would draw group cash, and whether that is a related-party use of cash is not established.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence for lower risk is that all eight directors are non-executive, the audit committee consists only of independent directors and reviews related-party transactions, the auditor reported effective internal control, no amendment, priming or exchange affecting creditors is documented, and management has set a year-end 2026 leverage target of below 2.5x. The view would move to Low if the target is met while dividends stay within equity free cash flow, if the debt documents show restricted-payment limits that bind the shareholder, and if the Chile options are priced and funded without recourse to the group. It would move to High if declared dividends continue to exceed internally generated cash, if distributions or related-party funding are paid from new borrowing, or if the controlling shareholder's holding passes 50% and the group elects controlled-company exemptions.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Between October 2025 and April 2026 the group completed six acquisitions or buy-outs that together changed its scale, and it sold most of its tower portfolio. Uruguay (enterprise value USD 440 million, closed 7 October 2025) and Ecuador (enterprise value USD 380 million, closed 30 October 2025) added mobile operators and their debt and leases. In Colombia the group bought out its partner's UNE shares for about USD 571 million on 29 January 2026, acquired Telefonica's 67.5% of Coltel for about USD 214.4 million on 6 February 2026, of which USD 169 million had been paid at that date, and bought the remaining Coltel shares on 27 April 2026. Coltel brought USD 1,424 million of other debt and financing and USD 515 million of lease liabilities.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The Chile entry in February 2026 was a joint acquisition with NJJ Cactus, a partner the filings do not describe as related: the vehicle paid USD 50 million at closing, carries contingent earn-outs without recourse to Millicom that the annual report caps at USD 150 million and the nine-month report at USD 490 million, and has an outstanding earn-out liability of USD 110 million funded by the vehicle's own debt. On the disposal side, the Lati tower sale to SBA and Atis Group brought total consideration of about USD 975 million and a gain of USD 741 million but created about USD 680 million of new lease assets and liabilities, and the sale of the Paraguay mobile finance business was agreed in January 2026 for a base price of USD 10 million.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: New debt in 2026 included a COP 370,000 million eight-year private bond subscribed by the Inter-American Development Bank and Proparco on 27 March, an USD 87.5 million reopening of the 2032 senior notes on 14 April, and a series of variable-rate loans at Coltel and Tigo Colombia, while Tigo Paraguay redeemed its 2027 senior unsecured notes for about USD 139.7 million on 29 April. The debt effects are measured by Financial foundation; the governance point here is that most new borrowing sits at operating companies in local currency and some carries parent guarantees.

fields.value: Sponsor / Governance Risk Level: Medium. The risk level is driven by concentrated control and distributions that are large against free cash flow, because payouts and acquisitions compete with debt reduction for the same cash, which implies slower deleveraging and some exposure to shareholder priorities. Countervailing evidence is an independent audit committee, effective internal control, regular disclosure and no documented creditor-adverse action. Governance and sponsor assessment completed with limitations; key gaps are the debt documents, the Iliad Holding payable and the controlling shareholder's later holdings.

fields.value: MILLICOM INTERNATIONAL CELLULAR SA (issuer id tigo), as of 2026-11-05, on the credit snapshot pathway (full credit assessment). The scope is Fundamental credit: the integrated view of business quality, cash generation, liquidity, refinancing capacity and financial policy, built from the four supplied filings and the three earlier modules.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Millicom presents an adequate credit profile, with strong margins and a larger operating base, but creditors carry leverage that rose with acquisitions, dividends that absorb most free cash flow and earnings concentrated in two countries.

fields.value: Adjusted EBITDA margin was 45.9% for nine months 2026 and equity free cash flow was USD 867 million, yet declared dividends were 0.87x of that cash flow and the issuer's own net leverage was 2.53x against a year-end target below 2.5x. Liquidity rests on a revolving facility whose availability after 2025 is not established, and no debt documents were supplied, so protections for creditors are not established.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The business is adequate to strong because margins are high and the base is spread over eleven markets, but nearly all recent growth was bought. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 45.9% for nine months 2026, down from 47.3%, and postpaid customers were 30.79% of mobile customers against 21.10% a year earlier, which makes revenue more recurring. Reported revenue rose 55.2% while organic growth was 4.4%, so the larger scale mostly reflects Coltel, Ecuador and Uruguay and favourable currency moves rather than a stronger market position. The consequence for creditors is that earnings quality has to be judged on the organic rate and on how much of the acquired EBITDA turns into cash.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Leverage is moderate on the statements but has risen faster than the headline suggests. Net debt before derivatives was USD 7,800 million, or 2.05x last-twelve-month reported EBITDA, at 30 September 2026, against 1.83x at the end of 2025. Pro forma net debt would be USD 8,379 million, or 2.20x, once the dividend payable of USD 579 million is settled in cash from the October 2026 instalment onwards, and the 15 October 2026 Coltel loan swap leaves it at USD 7,800 million, or 2.05x; pro forma cash after the dividend settlement is not established. The issuer's own net leverage, which adds derivatives and vendor financing, deducts lease costs and is pro forma for acquisitions, was 2.53x against 2.17x at the end of 2025. A lease liability of USD 3,190 million and capital expenditure payables of USD 2,101 million sit outside debt, so creditors face more fixed claims than the ratio shows.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Cash generation is solid but largely distributed, so deleveraging depends on the dividend as much as on operations. Equity free cash flow was USD 867 million, up 36.0% from USD 638 million, yet it equals only 29.31% of Adjusted EBITDA against 32.48% a year earlier, mainly because lease payments of USD 483 million and finance charges of USD 432 million together took 30.93% of Adjusted EBITDA against 28.26%. Declared dividends of USD 755 million were 0.87x equity free cash flow and left only USD 112 million, so cash cannot reduce debt materially while the payout continues.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Liquidity is the weakest dimension. Cash of USD 848 million was 0.97x the USD 872 million of debt due within one year, against 4.72x at the end of 2025, with USD 986 million due in the following year, and the USD 600 million revolving facility matures in October 2027 with its availability after 2025 not established. Funding access is nonetheless real: during 2026 the group raised development-bank and bond funding, reopened its 2032 senior notes and added bank loans in several countries, and the annual report records a Moody's rating of Ba2 with a stable outlook and a Fitch rating of BB+ at year-end 2025. The consequence is that refinancing depends on market and bank access staying open for about USD 1,858 million over two years, with no committed cushion shown for the period after 2025.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Earnings are concentrated, and currency moves flatter reported growth. Guatemala and Colombia together supplied 58.69% of segment revenue and 56.01% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, and the annual report states that group cash flow is highly dependent on Guatemala. The Colombian peso, Paraguayan guarani and Bolivian boliviano rose 25.4%, 22.7% and 17.1% against the US dollar over the year, which lifted reported results, while costs, capital expenditure and 38.99% of debt are in US dollars. A reversal would cut earnings in dollars, partly offset by a smaller dollar value of local-currency debt, but would leave dollar debt and dollar costs unchanged.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Financial policy is the main judgemental drag, consistent with a Medium sponsor and governance risk. One family group holds 42.2% of the voting shares and four of eight directors are affiliated with it, shareholders approved dividends of USD 3.00 per share payable to April 2027 and the board added an interim USD 1.50 per share, and the senior management plan communicated in October 2026 rewards equity free cash flow of USD 2 billion with no leverage condition stated. Policy therefore leaves the outcome for creditors to the board's discretion rather than to a documented restriction.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Colombia is the swing factor for the next two years. It is now the largest segment at 38.37% of segment revenue but earned a nine-month Adjusted EBITDA margin of 38.65% against 56.09% in Guatemala, after one-off costs of USD 116 million in nine months, and it faces competitors with substantially greater resources, including América Móvil, and a regulator that may impose asymmetric rules on a larger market share. If integration savings arrive the margin gap narrows and cash conversion improves; if competition forces price cuts the gap persists on the largest revenue base.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence for a better view is that the issuer's net leverage fell from 2.73x at June 2026 to 2.53x at September 2026, that 2026 equity free cash flow guidance was raised to around USD 1.1 billion and the year-end target lowered to below 2.5x, that interest is covered 4.58x by reported EBITDA, that 61.01% of debt is in local currencies that match revenue, and that dividends are discretionary rather than contractual and fell from 1.65x of equity free cash flow in nine months 2025 to 0.87x. The view would improve to a strong profile if year-end leverage comes in below 2.5x with dividends covered by equity free cash flow and the revolving facility is confirmed undrawn. It would weaken if equity free cash flow falls below declared dividends, if year-end leverage stays above 2.5x, if a Colombian price war or a currency reversal cuts Adjusted EBITDA, or if refinancing of the USD 1,858 million due within two years is delayed or priced above the issuer's average interest rate of 8.3%.

fields.value: The first strength is margin. Adjusted EBITDA margin of 45.9% for nine months 2026 means each dollar of revenue leaves a large cushion for lease, interest and tax charges, which is why interest cover stays at 4.58x despite higher debt; the margin is down from 47.3% a year earlier on acquisitions, so the cushion is thinner than before.

fields.value: The second strength is a more recurring revenue base. Postpaid customers rose to 30.79% of mobile customers, and prepaid customers, who buy short packages and sign no contract, are being migrated, which supports revenue visibility and lowers churn exposure in Guatemala, Panama and Paraguay.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The third strength is funding access matched to local revenue. 61.01% of gross debt is in local currencies, and 2026 saw a development-bank bond, a reopening of the 2032 senior notes and local bank loans, so the group can raise money across currencies, which reduces the risk that one market closes refinancing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The fourth strength is rising cash generation. Equity free cash flow rose 36.0% to USD 867 million, guidance for 2026 was raised to around USD 1.1 billion, and issuer net leverage fell from 2.73x to 2.53x in the third quarter, which shows that operations can reduce leverage when dividends are covered.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The first weakness is concentration. Guatemala and Colombia supply 56.01% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, so a shock in either market reaches the cash that services debt and funds dividends.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The second weakness is liquidity against maturities. Cash of USD 848 million is 0.97x the debt due in a year, so the group relies on refinancing and on a revolving facility whose availability is not established.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The third weakness is distributions: declared dividends were 0.87x equity free cash flow, which slows deleveraging and lets a controlling shareholder's priorities shape credit outcomes.

fields.value: The fifth weakness is the quality of growth. Reported revenue rose 55.2% against 4.4% organically, integration cost USD 149 million of one-off items in nine months and acquired businesses have provisional accounting, so a faster slowdown than organic trends would be a surprise only to those reading reported growth.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Millicom sells mobile and fixed services under the Tigo brand in eleven Latin American markets, and mobile generated 60% of 2025 service revenue with fixed and other services at 38%. Postpaid and fixed subscriptions give recurring monthly revenue, whereas prepaid customers buy packages that expire after days to weeks, so the postpaid share, 30.79% of mobile customers, matters for cash-flow visibility. Most towers were sold and leased back, which cut capital intensity but converted it into 15-year lease obligations, so lease payments were USD 483 million in nine months 2026, and Coltel added a large share of the mobile customer base in 2026. The consequence is a business with recurring revenue and heavy fixed charges, where debt service capacity depends on keeping the postpaid base and the margin.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Atlas Investissement, ultimately owned by the Niel family, holds 42.2% of the voting shares and four of eight directors are affiliated with it, so one holder can influence director elections and corporate actions without owning a majority. The Luxembourg parent depends on subsidiaries to send it cash, and about 70% of gross debt sits at the operating entities with the other 30% at corporate level, so parent creditors rank behind operating-company lenders except where the parent guarantees that debt, and guarantees and legal rank are not established. The Honduras joint venture, in which Millicom holds 66.67%, carries its own debt without recourse to the parent. The consequence is that cash reaching parent creditors depends on dividends and repatriation from subsidiaries, with USD 79 million repatriated from joint ventures and associates in nine months 2026, and on board decisions influenced by the largest shareholder.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Revenue is predictable in postpaid, fixed and business-to-business lines and cyclical in prepaid and equipment sales. Organic service revenue grew 5.3% in nine months 2026, helped by a more-for-more pricing strategy that raised mobile ARPU 19.0% in dollars, including currency effects, to USD 7.4 per month excluding Coltel, and postpaid customers excluding acquisitions grew. Fixed revenue is weaker underneath: excluding acquisitions the fixed revenue generating units would have declined because fixed telephony is shrinking, and home ARPU rose to USD 27.7 per month while the base would be shrinking without acquisitions. Competition on price and customer experience in markets with penetration above 100% limits further volume growth, so pricing power is moderate and the revenue outlook rests on mix migration rather than subscriber growth.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Direct costs grew faster than revenue in the third quarter, up 72.4% against revenue growth of 60.8%, on acquisitions, bad debt and World Cup programming, while operating expenses rose 57.4% including USD 20 million of Colombian restructuring. Severance of about USD 111 million was recorded in Colombia, and one-off items above Adjusted EBITDA were USD 149 million for nine months. Lease, interest and spectrum charges sit below Adjusted EBITDA and do not flex with volume, so the cash margin after them is more sensitive than the EBITDA margin: Adjusted EBITDA margin fell from 47.3% to 45.9%, or 1.4 percentage points, in nine months even with 5.3% organic service revenue growth. Margins can be defended against volume pressure only if integration savings arrive; the filings state no savings target, so resilience is not established beyond the Guatemala margin of 56.09%, which includes a one-time reversal of legal provisions in the third quarter.

fields.value: Capital expenditure excluding spectrum was USD 757 million and spectrum paid USD 207 million in nine months 2026, together 14.97% of revenue, and fixed commitments to buy network equipment and intangibles were USD 384 million, of which USD 367 million fall due within a year against USD 305 million at the end of 2025. Equity free cash flow converted 29.31% of Adjusted EBITDA, down from 32.48%, because lease payments, finance charges and USD 306 million of taxes rose with the perimeter. Colombian spectrum payables of USD 662 million at the end of 2025 fall due in instalments to 2037. Capex can be deferred in the near term, but spectrum and lease charges cannot, so the cash that supports debt service is what remains after fixed charges, and it is already largely paid out in dividends.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Rivalry is intense: the annual report names América Móvil, Telefónica and Liberty Latin America as main competitors with greater resources, adds WOM in Colombia, where competitors may hold a dominant position, and describes telecom services as largely commoditized, so competition on price can compress margin and raise churn. Entry is limited by the need for spectrum licences with fixed terms, which is an analyst inference, and several licences expire from 2026. Substitution is a risk mainly for pay-TV through wireless and satellite alternatives and for fixed telephony. Buyers have little to hold them in prepaid, where no contract is signed, but credit exposure to certain business customers, mainly governments, is concentrated. Suppliers matter through spectrum fees, the tower leaseback and programming content such as the World Cup. The consequence is that pricing power is clearest in Guatemala, where ARPU rose and margin is highest, and weakest in Colombia, the largest market.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: These factors are material, so they are included. The strongest is currency: the Colombian peso, guarani and boliviano rose against the dollar over the year, which flattered reported revenue and profit while also raising the dollar value of local-currency debt, while the annual report warns that a significant amount of costs, capital expenditure and borrowings is in dollars. Bolivia moved from a fixed peg to a market regime and foreign exchange volatility remains elevated there. Higher energy prices from the Middle East conflict add inflation and cost pressure. On regulation, spectrum licences must be renewed against fees, the Costa Rican regulator blocked the planned merger and a USD 32 million goodwill impairment followed, and tax claims against subsidiaries are estimated at USD 378 million with provisions of USD 60 million. The consequence is that currency and regulation can move earnings and leverage in dollars without any change in operating performance.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths are the 45.9% margin, scale across eleven markets, a rising postpaid share and funding in several currencies. Weaknesses are concentration in Guatemala and Colombia, cash of USD 848 million against USD 872 million of debt due in a year, distributions that absorb 0.87x of free cash flow and claims outside debt. Opportunities that could improve credit quality are integration savings in Colombia, a partial sale of the mobile financial services business and a leverage target below 2.5x. Threats that could weaken it are a Colombian price war, currency reversal, regulatory asymmetry and a further large acquisition or related-party commitment.

fields.value: For the next twelve to twenty-four months, management guides to equity free cash flow of around USD 1.1 billion for 2026, which implies about USD 233 million in the fourth quarter after USD 867 million in nine months, and to year-end leverage below 2.5x. On the issuer's own figures, leverage of 2.53x needs net debt about USD 95 million lower, and the fourth-quarter cash left, if the October dividend matches the USD 126 million paid in the third quarter, is about USD 107 million, so headroom against the target is thin at roughly USD 12 million before currency effects and payments for acquisitions. Tailwinds are integration savings, higher postpaid mix and local-currency strength; headwinds are the World Cup content boost to home revenue, which is unlikely to recur, USD 1.50 per share of additional dividends in January and April 2027, spectrum payments, the maturity of the revolving facility in October 2027 and Chile losses. Over three to five years, maturities are USD 1,947 million in the third year, USD 1,601 million in the fourth and USD 1,147 million in the fifth, with USD 2,094 million after five years, and a management plan pays about USD 50 million only when equity free cash flow reaches USD 2 billion a year. The path to a stronger profile is therefore deleveraging through free cash flow growth, which depends on the board holding the dividend.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The most plausible downside is a price war and asymmetric regulation in Colombia during integration, coinciding with a reversal of local currencies. The operating break comes first in Colombian ARPU and postpaid growth, where a competitor with a dominant position could cut prices. Revenue then grows below the 5.3% organic rate and Adjusted EBITDA margin falls because network and integration costs do not flex, while lease payments and finance charges of USD 915 million in nine months remain fixed claims on the cash that is left. Free cash flow falls below the dividend, and as an illustration each 10% fall in last-twelve-month reported EBITDA lifts net debt over EBITDA from 2.05x to 2.27x and a 20% fall lifts it to 2.56x. Liquidity is then tested by USD 872 million of maturities against cash of USD 848 million, a revolving facility that matures in October 2027 and USD 986 million due the year after. Management can cut or defer dividends that are not yet declared, defer capital expenditure, sell the mobile financial services business and draw development-bank funding, and market access in 2026 shows these routes are open. Resilience therefore appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress within twelve months if refinancing stays available, but not if the revolving facility is drawn, because the cushion would then be gone. The observable triggers are Colombian service revenue growth, the margin, free cash flow against dividends and the refinancing of the next two years of maturities.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Overall, Millicom presents an adequate business profile supported by high margins, scale in eleven markets and a rising postpaid base, but credit quality is constrained by acquisition-driven leverage, dividends that absorb 0.87x of equity free cash flow and earnings concentrated in Guatemala and Colombia. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because equity free cash flow is growing and guidance was raised, but it is thin after fixed charges and distributions. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on bank and development-bank access, on confirmation that the revolving facility is available and on the board holding the dividend while leverage falls to the target. The primary downside path is a Colombian price war and currency reversal that cut earnings while leases, interest and dividends continue. Further analysis would require the debt documents, the revolving facility's status, instrument-level terms and pro forma earnings of the acquired businesses. Fundamental credit analysis completed. Top risk: concentration of earnings combined with distributions that leave little cash for deleveraging.
